name: Meher Bano

portrait.alt: Placeholder portrait for Meher Bano — hands setting enamel

summary: Meher fires colour into metal the way her grandmother taught her: slowly, in layers, and never in a hurry to finish.
quote: Purple is the hardest colour to fire. It goes brown if you rush it. So you learn not to rush.
story: Meher Bano grew up in a lane in Jaipur where the sound of small hammers starts before the sound of traffic. Her grandmother was an enameller; her mother set stones. By twelve, Meher could do both, and by twenty she had decided she would do them differently.

Traditional meenakari hides its colour on the back of a piece, a secret for the wearer. Meher likes bringing it to the front. When Pratima arrived with sketches of jhumkas that 'wanted to be lilac, not ruby', Meher laughed — and then spent three weeks getting the purple right.
Today she runs a small studio of four women. Every Nemara enamel piece passes through their kiln, one firing at a time.

name: Ramesh Soni

portrait.alt: Placeholder portrait for Ramesh Soni — hands twisting silver wire

summary: Ramesh draws with wire. A single filigree collar can hold four hundred hand-twisted coils, each one soldered by eye.
quote: People think filigree is decoration. It is structure. The lace is what holds the shape.
story: Cuttack's filigree workers call the finest wire 'hair'. Ramesh Soni has been twisting it for thirty-one years, first in his uncle's workshop and now in his own, a room with one window and very good light.

Most of his work used to be for temple and wedding orders: heavy, symmetrical, exact. Nemara asked him for something he says he had never been asked for — asymmetry. 'Pratima drew one hoop bigger than the other and said, this is on purpose. I liked her immediately.'
His filigree gives Nemara pieces their lightness: they look sculptural and weigh almost nothing.

name: Lakshmi Narayanan

portrait.alt: Placeholder portrait for Lakshmi Narayanan — hands chasing a metal sheet

summary: Lakshmi pushes pictures into metal from behind — courtyards, lamps, temple doors — until the flat sheet remembers them.
quote: A motif is a memory with a shape. I just press it in until it stays.
story: Lakshmi Narayanan trained in temple jewellery, the kind made for festivals and brides. She still makes those. But on Thursdays, she says, she makes 'the new things' — the Nemara pieces that take old motifs somewhere they haven't been.
Repoussé is worked from the back: the metal is set on a bed of pitch and coaxed outward with blunt tools, one small push at a time. A single kada can take two days of pressing before it is polished.
Her courtyard motif on the Aangan kada is drawn from the house she grew up in, which no longer stands. 'Now it does,' she says, 'on someone's wrist.'

name: Farida Qureshi

portrait.alt: Placeholder portrait for Farida Qureshi — hands polishing cast brass

summary: Farida finishes brass by hand until it feels warm before you put it on. Her pieces are the ones Nemara wears every day.
quote: Machines make it shiny. Hands make it soft. You can feel the difference with your eyes closed.
story: Moradabad has made brass for the world for centuries — mostly bowls, lamps and trophies. Farida Qureshi was the first woman in her family's workshop to work the metal rather than pack it.

She casts in small batches and finishes every piece herself: filing, hammering, polishing with walnut shell and, finally, her own thumb. Her hammered textures are irregular on purpose. 'If it's perfect,' she says, 'it looks like it came from nowhere.'
Farida makes Nemara's everyday line, the pieces designed to be worn to work, to the market, to sleep if you forget.
